bull.b: Revenue exceeding four times the prior-year level indicates strong demand across multiple program areas rather than reliance on a single lunar mission. If execution continues, this expanding base can improve operating leverage, strengthen customer relationships, and support sustained scale over the next several quarters.

The record backlog provides meaningful forward revenue visibility, while its mix across civil, commercial and national security customers reduces dependence on one funding source. More than 80 spacecraft under contract also supports production scale and a broader competitive position.

The swing to positive gross profit and the narrower adjusted EBITDA loss show improving economics as revenue scales. Management’s reaffirmed expectation for positive adjusted EBITDA in 2026 suggests the business may be progressing toward better cost absorption and a more sustainable operating model.

bear.b: Negative equity combined with materially higher debt leaves the company with limited financial flexibility and a structurally strained capital base. This can increase reliance on external funding, raise refinancing risk, and constrain investment choices if operating performance or contract timing weakens.

Ongoing negative operating and free cash flow means growth is consuming substantial capital rather than funding expansion internally. Continued investment, mission spending and working-capital needs could require additional financing before the company reaches cash-flow breakeven, increasing financial risk.

bear.t: Ongoing Losses and Program Cost Pressure
bear.b: Despite better gross profit, the company remains loss-making and the IM-4 estimate-at-complete adjustment demonstrates that individual programs can generate unexpected cost pressure. Such adjustments may delay profitability, reduce cash conversion, and make earnings less predictable as the mission portfolio expands.
